calib.source: 2020 -> 2024 change, final early vote vs presidential margin

notes.PA: No in-person early voting, so this is mail ballots returned. Pennsylvania's mail electorate is heavily Democratic whatever the year (about D+53 at this point in 2022, when Republicans won the national House vote by 3), so it says little about direction; the slope fitted for mail-only states is small for that reason. Requests by party are shown for context.
notes.FL: Mail plus in-person. In-person early voting opens Oct 19 (Oct 24 in 2022, Oct 21 in 2024); until then this is mail only, and Florida Republicans moved toward mail after 2022. Florida's final early vote was R+6 in 2022 (result R+19) and R+9 in 2024 (result R+13).
notes.NV: Mail plus in-person, from the Secretary of State's daily files (UF Election Lab compiles them; Jon Ralston's blog reported the 2022 and 2024 leads used here). In-person opens Oct 17. 2022's early vote finished about D+1.5 and the Senate race was D+0.8; 2024's finished R+3.8 and the presidential race was R+3.1.
notes.CO: All-mail state; nearly every ballot is returned by mail or drop box. The Secretary of State posts a release each weekday from about three weeks out with returns by party; 2022 and 2024 points come from those spreadsheets.
notes.IA: Absentee ballots received, which in Iowa include ballots cast in person at the auditor's office. Iowa Democrats vote absentee far more than Republicans in every year (2022's absentee pool was D+19 while the Senate race was R+12), so the small mail-state slope applies. 2022 and 2024 points are the Secretary of State's daily reports as compiled by Bleeding Heartland.
notes.AZ: Early ballots returned, compiled from county reports by Stealth Analytics for UF Election Lab (Arizona has no official statewide daily file). No same-point baseline yet; the 2022 and 2024 final early votes are shown for context.

story.headline: Against the same point in 2024, every comparable measure is more Democratic. Against 2022, mail volume is down in Wisconsin and North Carolina and flat in Michigan, while Georgia's first day of in-person voting ran well ahead of 2022's. Democrats have moved from mail ballots to voting early in person, which bends both comparisons.

story.compare_note: Democratic share of mail-ballot requests (CNN/Catalist, Oct 1). Gray dot is the same point in 2024. Virginia's early voters with only Democratic primary history lead those with only GOP history by 18 points, vs. 8 in 2024; Ohio's early electorate is about 27 points more Democratic than at this point in 2024 (CNN, Oct 11). North Carolina's comparison is computed from the State Board of Elections' files. CNN also found that the 2022 request pools were more Democratic than 2026's in every listed state except Iowa.

bullets.title: Georgia's first day of in-person voting beat 2022's by more than 50,000.
bullets.html: More than 188,000 Georgians voted in person on Oct 13, more than 53,000 above the first day of early voting in the 2022 midterm (the Secretary of State's office put that day at over 135,000). Tuesday beat every 2022 early-voting day except the last. Mail is small: about 130,000 absentee ballots requested, with 10,200 returned, against nearly 286,000 requested by the end of 2022.

bullets.title: Ohio shows the mode shift in official numbers.
bullets.html: Through Oct 13, Ohio counted 194,841 early in-person votes and 33,629 returned mail ballots. At the same point in 2022 the Secretary of State reported 50,368 in-person votes and 871,041 mail requests; this year's requests stand at about 631,000. CNN's Oct 11 analysis put the early electorate about 27 points more Democratic than at this point in 2024.
bullets.aff: Official data; CNN is a nonpartisan outlet

bullets.title: The edge over 2024 is real but partly a change in how Democrats vote.
bullets.html: Democratic mail requests in North Carolina are down 40% from 2022, against 18% for Republicans, yet Democrats are returning ballots faster (22% returned vs. 17% in 2022). In an NBC poll, 23% of Democrats plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in 2024, and 36% plan to vote early in person, up from 30%. Democrats' confidence that the Postal Service will deliver ballots on time fell from 86% to 60% (Marist).

bullets.title: Wisconsin's mail vote is down 30% on 2022; Michigan's has flattened.
bullets.html: Wisconsin clerks had received about 128,000 absentee ballots three weeks out, against nearly 184,000 at the same point in 2022; Madison fell from about 31,700 to about 9,000, which Dane County's clerk attributes to distrust of the Postal Service. Michigan's returned absentee ballots (440,677 on Oct 13) are only slightly above the same point in 2022 (432,960), though requests are up more than 20% because of the permanent mail list. Neither state registers voters by party.

bullets.title: Florida Democrats lead the mail vote, as they usually do before in-person voting opens.
bullets.html: As of Tuesday morning, just over 226,000 mail ballots had come back from registered Democrats, nearly 190,000 from Republicans and nearly 98,000 from voters with no party; about 1.77 million more are outstanding (nearly 760,000 sent to Democrats, 600,000 to Republicans). Republicans typically make up the difference when in-person early voting opens Oct 24.

bullets.title: Democratic data firms report a Latino and Black surge.
bullets.html: TargetSmart's Tom Bonier says the Hispanic share of the early vote is above the same point in 2022 in more than 94% of 229 comparable counties, with about 112,000 Latino early votes vs. 106,000 at this point in 2024. No independent replication yet.

bullets.title: Republicans say they vote later.
bullets.html: National Review's Noah Rothman argues Democrats will lead the early vote, "but perhaps not by the margins the party expects," because their own warnings eroded trust in mail. Wisconsin's GOP reads the Madison and Milwaukee declines as "a lack of enthusiasm among Dem voters"; the state Democratic Party notes absentee voting also fell about 23% from 2020 to 2024. No quantitative RNC early-vote claims for 2026 turned up.
bullets.aff: GOP-aligned claims, reported by nonpartisan outlets

bullets.title: Nevada is the cautionary tale.
bullets.html: By the afternoon of Oct 13 just under 6,000 ballots had been accepted, about 0.3% of active voters, with Democrats about 15 points ahead of Republicans (2,229 to 1,298 in the morning count, with 1,163 nonpartisans). Jon Ralston says about 5,000 ballots is not a statistically significant sample. In 2024 Democrats led Nevada's mail vote, Republicans led the total early vote, and Trump won.

story.calendar_note: Georgia's in-person early voting opened Oct 13; Iowa and Kansas mail ballots go out Oct 14; North Carolina's one-stop voting opens Oct 15. Colorado mailed its ballots Oct 2-9; Oct 19 is when its voter service centers must open. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
story.cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 37 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 9-14) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
story.signals_verdict: Against 2024 the early vote looks more Democratic; against 2022 the mail vote is down in Wisconsin and North Carolina and flat in Michigan, while Georgia's first day of in-person voting ran about 40% above 2022's. All of it is bent by Democrats moving from mail to voting in person, so the early vote is consistent with the polls rather than ahead of them. The next real tests are North Carolina's one-stop voting from Oct 15 and a full week of Georgia's in-person numbers.

signals.title: Georgia's first day of in-person voting ran well ahead of 2022
signals.value: More than 188,000 in-person votes on Oct 13, more than 53,000 above the first day of 2022 (the Secretary of State put 2022's first day at over 135,000). About 130,000 mail ballots requested vs. nearly 286,000 by the end of 2022.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. Part of the in-person surge is voters who would have used mail; the 2024 first day was over 300,000.
signals.src: FOX 5 Atlanta and WTOC, using Georgia Secretary of State data, Oct 13-14

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate is far more Democratic than in 2024
signals.value: About 27 points more Democratic than at this point in 2024, by primary history. Counties Trump won by 20+ are R+5, vs. R+30 then. Official count through Oct 13: 194,841 in person (50,368 at the same point in 2022) and 33,629 mail ballots returned.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to in person: mail requests are about 631,000 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022.
signals.src: CNN, Oct 11; Ohio Secretary of State, Oct 13

signals.title: Virginia's early voters lean further Democratic than in 2024
signals.value: Voters with only Democratic primary history lead those with only GOP history by 18 points, vs. 8 at this point in 2024. In VA-1: D+15, vs. about R+3.
signals.catch: Primary history isn't a vote, and 2024 had a presidential-year electorate.

signals.title: Democrats are returning their ballots faster than in 2022
signals.value: North Carolina: 22% of Democrats' requested ballots are back, vs. 17% at this point in 2022. Pennsylvania: 20% vs. 15%.
signals.catch: It could be enthusiasm, or worry that the mail will be slow; NBC/Penn say the data can't tell yet.

signals.title: Democrats' share of mail requests is up from 2024
signals.value: Iowa 67% vs. 54% at the same point in 2024; North Carolina 42% vs. 36%; Pennsylvania 66% vs. 62%; Maine 57% vs. 53%.
signals.catch: Against 2022 the same shares are lower everywhere except Iowa (see the other column).

signals.title: Florida Democrats lead the returned mail vote
signals.value: Just over 226,000 mail ballots from Democrats vs. nearly 190,000 from Republicans and nearly 98,000 from no-party voters, as of Oct 13.
signals.catch: No same-point comparison yet; Republicans hold a registration edge of more than a million and typically make up the difference when in-person early voting opens Oct 24.
signals.src: Tallahassee Reports, using Division of Elections data, Oct 14
signals.aff: Official data via a local outlet

signals.title: Trump country in New Jersey is voting less Republican
signals.value: In counties Trump won by 20+, the pre-election vote has shifted nearly 11 points toward Democrats vs. this point in 2024.
signals.catch: Small counties and a presidential-year baseline.

signals.title: Wisconsin's mail vote is running 30% behind 2022
signals.value: About 128,000 absentee ballots returned three weeks out, vs. nearly 184,000 at the same point in 2022. Madison: about 9,000 vs. about 31,700.
signals.catch: No party registration; the Dane County clerk blames distrust of the Postal Service, and in-person absentee voting doesn't start until Oct 20.
signals.src: WPR, using Wisconsin Elections Commission data, Oct 13

signals.title: Michigan's mail returns have fallen back to the 2022 pace
signals.value: 440,677 ballots returned by Oct 13, vs. 432,960 at the same point in 2022; a week earlier returns were 30% ahead. Requests are up more than 20% (2,083,240 vs. 1,707,970).
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. About 95% of requests come from the permanent mail list; in-person early voting opens Oct 24.

signals.title: Against 2022, Democrats' share of mail requests is down
signals.value: Lower now than at this point in 2022 in every state CNN checked except Iowa.
signals.catch: Democrats are moving from mail to early in-person voting: 23% plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in 2024 (NBC poll).

signals.title: North Carolina Democrats requested far fewer mail ballots
signals.value: Requests vs. the same point in 2022: Democrats down 42%, Republicans down 19%.
signals.catch: Same mode shift. North Carolina's in-person early voting, where most of its vote is cast, starts Oct 15.

signals.title: Pennsylvania Republicans are requesting more mail ballots
signals.value: Requests vs. the same point in 2022: Republicans up 18%, Democrats down 14%.
signals.catch: Republicans have been urged to vote by mail this year, so more requests may be a change of method rather than more voters.

signals.title: Georgia's mail requests fell more in Democratic areas
signals.value: Down 52% in heavily Harris precincts vs. 39% in heavily Trump precincts.
signals.catch: Mail is about 5% of Georgia's vote; the first day of in-person voting (Oct 13) ran well ahead of 2022.

watch.trail_note: Trump and Vance campaign appearances since Sep 1, 2026, from White House pool reports, Roll Call Factbase and local coverage. Closed-press fundraisers and tele-rallies are rarely reported, so they are undercounted.

happened.title: Senate Majority PAC adds to Michigan and Maine, pauses Georgia and North Carolina
happened.what: Senate Majority PAC is adding $3.7 million in Michigan, bringing its total there to about $35 million, and $3 million in Maine, while pausing its ads in Georgia and North Carolina, where Jon Ossoff and Roy Cooper lead.
happened.why: Democrats' main Senate super PAC is treating Georgia and North Carolina as won and concentrating on the two Republican-held seats that would complete a net gain of four.

happened.title: GOP super PACs pull out of four House races, reinforce 16
happened.what: Congressional Leadership Fund canceled spending in IA-01, NJ-07, MI-08 and OH-01 and added money in 16 districts including PA-01, TX-15, WI-01, VA-01 and MI-04; a MAGA Inc. affiliate also pulled about $1 million meant to help Marty O'Donnell against Rep. Susie Lee in NV-03.
happened.why: House Republicans are conceding two of their own Trump-district seats and two Democratic targets to concentrate on districts Trump carried, narrowing their path to 218.

happened.title: Cook moves Alaska governor to Lean Democrat, three red states off Solid
happened.what: The Cook Political Report shifted the Alaska governor race from Toss Up to Lean Democrat, citing Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins' polling lead and a split Republican field, and moved Oklahoma, Nebraska and Vermont from Solid to Likely Republican.
happened.why: Cook says the shifts give Democrats a chance at a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010; its governor map now has four Toss Ups (Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Wisconsin).

happened.title: Senate Leadership Fund adds $8 million in Nebraska
happened.what: Senate Leadership Fund plans about $8 million in new Nebraska spending through Election Day on top of $7 million already spent to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts against independent Dan Osborn, and the crypto PAC Fairshake began a $7 million Nebraska campaign.
happened.why: Republicans are now spending to hold a seat Trump carried by about 20 points, money that cannot go to Kansas, Iowa, Ohio or Texas.

happened.title: Ossoff, Collins clash over son-in-law and Epstein in final debate
happened.what: In the Atlanta Press Club debate, Sen. Jon Ossoff demanded that Rep. Mike Collins stop his son-in-law from producing what Ossoff called neo-Nazi content from Collins' home, while Collins attacked Ossoff over donor Reid Hoffman's ties to Jeffrey Epstein and would not say directly whether Biden won in 2020.
happened.why: It was the last debate in one of the few Democratic-held Senate seats Republicans are contesting, on the first day of Georgia's early voting.

happened.title: Hinson breaks with Trump on Russian diesel in final Iowa debate
happened.what: In the second and last Hinson-Turek debate, Rep. Ashley Hinson said she disagreed with Trump's deal easing sanctions on Russian diesel, while Josh Turek accused her of pushing Iowa toward a 'second farm crisis' through tariffs and Iran-war votes.
happened.why: Iowa's open Republican-held seat is a Cook Toss Up, and Hinson's distance from Trump on fuel prices shows where Republicans think the race is being lost.

happened.title: Collins, Jackson spar over Iran war funding in third Maine debate
happened.what: Troy Jackson said Sen. Susan Collins, as Appropriations chair, could defund the Iran war, while Collins said Jackson had filed no FEC reports and did not know Medicare from Medicaid; both opposed tariffs on Canada.
happened.why: Maine is a Republican-held seat central to a Democratic Senate majority, and a Suffolk poll released the same week had Jackson at 49-47.

happened.title: Sununu keeps Trump at arm's length in first New Hampshire debate
happened.what: In the first Pappas-Sununu Senate debate, in North Conway, John Sununu said he had opposed Trump in 2016 and 2024 and tied Chris Pappas to Biden, while Pappas accused Sununu of siding with drug companies; Pappas has agreed to two more debates.
happened.why: New Hampshire is the Democratic-held seat Republicans most need to flip, and Sununu's distance from Trump is their path in a state Harris carried.

happened.title: Trump endorses Tafoya in Minnesota and Wilson for Alaska governor
happened.what: Trump told his Youngstown rally to vote for Michele Tafoya, who has run as a pro-choice Republican independent of the president and called his rhetoric about Minnesota's Somali community inappropriate; on Oct 13 he endorsed Bernadette Wilson for Alaska governor and said he would not back Dave Bronson.
happened.why: The Minnesota endorsement undercuts Tafoya's distancing strategy in a race where Peggy Flanagan leads by four, and consolidating Republicans behind Wilson is the GOP's only path in Alaska's ranked-choice governor race.
happened.src: MPR News, Oct 13; Alaska's News Source, Oct 13

happened.title: Texas polls: Talarico narrowly ahead, Abbott edges back in front
happened.what: Marist (Oct 8-11) has James Talarico over Ken Paxton 47-45 among likely voters and Gov. Greg Abbott over Gina Hinojosa 49-45; Siena/ReconMR (Oct 5-8) has Talarico 48-44, down from a six-point lead in September, and Abbott 48-47 after trailing by four.
happened.why: Texas is still a live Senate pickup, but both polls show Republicans recovering, especially in the governor race Cook rates Lean Republican.

happened.title: Rick Jackson skips Atlanta Press Club governor debate
happened.what: Republican nominee Rick Jackson skipped the Atlanta Press Club debate to campaign with Gov. Brian Kemp near Augusta, the first general-election governor no-show since 1994; Keisha Lance Bottoms debated an empty podium for 30 minutes and called him a coward.
happened.why: Cook rates Georgia's open governorship a Toss Up, and the no-show gives Democrats a message in a race they need for a majority of governorships.

happened.title: Cook shifts 18 more House races toward Democrats
happened.what: The Cook Political Report moved 18 House races toward Democrats, including four Republican-held seats from Toss Up to Lean Democrat and four races from Lean Republican to Toss Up, and called a Democratic gain of nine to 19 seats the most likely outcome.
happened.why: That outcome would leave Democrats with 224 to 234 seats, above the 218 needed for a House majority.

upcoming.title: Iowa absentee voting begins
upcoming.what: Oct. 14 is the first day of absentee voting in Iowa, and the deadline to vote absentee in person is Nov. 2.
upcoming.why: Early ballots begin in Iowa's competitive Senate and governor races and in the IA-01, IA-02 and IA-03 House contests.
upcoming.src: Iowa Secretary of State (VoterReady), accessed Oct 13

upcoming.title: Alaska House candidates meet in 'Debate for the State'
upcoming.what: Alaska Public Media's Debate for the State features the U.S. House candidates from 7 to 8 p.m. Alaska time, on statewide radio, TV and alaskapublic.org.
upcoming.why: Rep. Nick Begich's at-large seat is one of the Republican-held seats Democrats are contesting in a state where the Senate race is a Toss-up.

upcoming.title: CNN town hall with Talarico in Fort Worth
upcoming.what: CNN and Jubilee Media host a town hall with Texas Senate nominee James Talarico in Fort Worth, moderated by Erin Burnett, live on CNN; Ken Paxton has accepted no debate invitation.
upcoming.why: Texas is a Republican-held seat on Democrats' path to a majority, with Talarico up two in Marist's Oct 8-11 poll.

upcoming.title: North Carolina one-stop early voting begins
upcoming.what: In-person early voting with same-day registration begins in North Carolina and runs through 3 p.m. on Oct. 31.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the open Senate race Cook now rates Likely Democrat and in competitive House districts such as NC-01 and NC-11.

upcoming.title: FEC third-quarter reports due
upcoming.what: House and Senate campaign committees must file October quarterly reports covering activity from July 1 through Sept. 30.
upcoming.why: The reports show how much cash each campaign has for the final three weeks.

upcoming.title: Benson, James hold second Michigan governor debate
upcoming.what: Democrat Jocelyn Benson and Republican John James meet for the second of two scheduled debates, at WDIV-TV in metro Detroit; no start time was listed.
upcoming.why: Michigan's governorship is open and on the competitive list.

upcoming.title: Alaska Senate candidates meet in 'Debate for the State'
upcoming.what: Alaska Public Media's Debate for the State features the top two U.S. Senate candidates from 7 to 8 p.m. Alaska time.
upcoming.why: Inside Elections rates the race between Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola a Toss-up, making Alaska a possible Democratic pickup.

upcoming.title: Vance rallies in Monroe, Michigan
upcoming.what: Vice President Vance headlines a Trump 47 Committee rally at the LevelUp Training Complex in Monroe, with doors at 10 a.m. and the program at noon.
upcoming.why: Michigan's open Senate seat is a Cook Toss Up, and Monroe County voted for Trump by 27 points in 2024.

upcoming.title: Final Collins-Jackson debate in Bangor
upcoming.what: Maine Public, NEWS CENTER Maine and the Portland Press Herald host a live 60-minute debate between Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson at the Gracie Theater in Bangor.
upcoming.why: It is the last scheduled debate in a close race for a Republican-held seat central to the Senate majority.

upcoming.title: Minnesota early voting on tabulators begins
upcoming.what: Minnesota's early voting period, in which ballots are fed directly into a counter, begins statewide and runs through Nov. 2; in-person absentee voting has been open since Sept. 18.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the Flanagan-Tafoya Senate race, which Inside Elections rates Lean Democrat, and in the MN-02 House race.
upcoming.src: Minnesota Secretary of State, accessed Oct 14

upcoming.title: Nevada early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early voting for the general election begins in Nevada and runs through Oct. 30.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in Nevada's governor race and in House seats including NV-02, which Democrats recently added to their target list.

upcoming.title: Texas early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early voting begins in Texas and runs through Oct. 30; the mail-ballot application deadline is Oct. 23.
upcoming.why: Ballots start banking in the Paxton-Talarico Senate race and a governor race Cook moved to Lean Republican on Oct. 1.

upcoming.title: Wisconsin in-person absentee voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person absentee voting begins in Wisconsin, with hours and locations set by municipal clerks.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the open Wisconsin governor race and in House battlegrounds such as WI-01.
upcoming.src: Wisconsin Examiner via News From The States, Sep 18

upcoming.title: Rogers, El-Sayed hold second Michigan Senate debate
upcoming.what: WXYZ-TV hosts the second debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed at its Broadcast House studios in Detroit, airing statewide; no start time was listed.
upcoming.why: It comes three days before statewide early voting begins in Michigan.

upcoming.title: Marshall, Hamilton debate on Kansas Nexstar stations
upcoming.what: Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton debate from 7 to 8 p.m. Central, originating at WDAF-TV in Kansas City and airing on Nexstar stations in Kansas City, Topeka, Wichita and Joplin.
upcoming.why: Cook rates the race a Toss Up, and both parties' main Senate super PACs are now spending on it.

upcoming.title: Crowley, Tiffany hold Wisconsin governor debate
upcoming.what: WISN-12 hosts a one-hour debate between Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany at Marquette University at 7 p.m. local time, also carried by partner stations in Green Bay, Madison, Wausau, Eau Claire and La Crosse.
upcoming.why: Tiffany has said one debate is sufficient, making this likely the only televised matchup in the open governor race.

upcoming.title: Sand, Lahn debate for Iowa governor
upcoming.what: Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn meet in a live 90-minute Iowa PBS debate at 7 p.m. Central.
upcoming.why: Iowa's open governorship is one of the competitive governor races.

upcoming.title: FEC pre-general reports due
upcoming.what: Pre-general reports covering Oct. 1 through Oct. 14 are due to the FEC.
upcoming.why: They provide the last full look at campaign and committee cash and spending before Election Day.

upcoming.title: Arizona mail-ballot request deadline
upcoming.what: Oct. 23 is the last day to request a mail ballot in Arizona; Oct. 27 is the last recommended day to mail it back, and in-person early voting ends Oct. 30.
upcoming.why: Arizona's governor race, rated Lean Democrat by Cook, and the AZ-01 and AZ-06 House seats are on the competitive list.

upcoming.title: Michigan statewide early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person voting sites open statewide in Michigan, open at least eight hours a day through Nov. 1, with some communities offering extra days.
upcoming.why: Early votes start in the open Senate and governor races and in House battlegrounds such as MI-04 and MI-07.

upcoming.title: Florida mandatory early voting begins
upcoming.what: Florida's mandatory early voting period runs Oct. 24 through Oct. 31, and counties may offer additional days or hours.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the Senate race, a governor race Cook moved to Lean Republican, and House seats such as FL-13 and FL-27.

upcoming.title: Pennsylvania mail ballot application deadline
upcoming.what: Oct. 27 is the deadline to apply for a mail-in or absentee ballot in Pennsylvania, and completed ballots must reach county election offices by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.
upcoming.why: Pennsylvania's House battlegrounds, including PA-01, PA-07 and PA-08, could help decide House control.
upcoming.src: Pennsylvania Department of State, accessed Oct 13

upcoming.title: Ohio absentee application deadline
upcoming.what: Absentee ballot applications must reach county boards by 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 27; early in-person voting runs extended hours Oct. 26-30, and mail ballots must arrive by 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 3.
upcoming.why: Ohio's Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown and its open governor race are both Cook Toss Ups.
upcoming.src: Ohio Secretary of State, accessed Oct 14

upcoming.title: Maine no-excuse absentee voting period ends
upcoming.what: Oct. 29 is the last day of Maine's no-excuse absentee period, including in-person absentee voting at town and city halls.
upcoming.why: The deadline shapes early ballots in the Collins-Jackson Senate race and the ME-02 House race.

upcoming.title: Nevada polls close; Alaska follows after midnight ET
upcoming.what: Polls close at 10 p.m. ET in Nevada and Montana; most of Alaska closes at midnight ET and the Aleutian Islands at 1 a.m. ET on Nov. 4.
upcoming.why: Alaska's Senate race, rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections, is likely to be among the last competitive contests to report.

upcoming.title: First polls close in Indiana and Kentucky
upcoming.what: Polls in the Eastern time portions of Indiana and Kentucky close at 6 p.m. ET, with the rest of both states closing at 7 p.m. ET.
upcoming.why: The first returns of the night include House races such as KY-06, which Inside Elections moved to Lean Republican.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia, most of Florida
upcoming.what: Polls close at 7 p.m. ET in Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia and Vermont, in most of Florida (the western Panhandle at 8 p.m. ET) and at most New Hampshire polling places (all by 8 p.m. ET).
upcoming.why: First returns arrive in the Georgia, South Carolina, Florida and New Hampshire Senate races and the Georgia and Florida governor races.

upcoming.title: Polls close in North Carolina and Ohio
upcoming.what: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.
upcoming.why: Results begin in the North Carolina and Ohio Senate races and the Ohio governor race.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Maine, Pennsylvania, most of Michigan, Texas
upcoming.what: Polls close at 8 p.m. ET in Maine, Pennsylvania and the rest of New Hampshire, and in most of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, whose westernmost areas close at 9 p.m. ET.
upcoming.why: First results arrive in the Maine, Michigan, Texas and Kansas Senate races and the Michigan and Texas governor races.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Arizona
upcoming.what: Polls close at 9 p.m. ET in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin and Arizona.
upcoming.why: Results begin in the Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska Senate races and the Iowa, Wisconsin and Arizona governor races.

comps.label: Approval and the midterm swing
comps.note: Midterms since 1950: the president's party loses ground, more when the president is unpopular. Trump's net approval is −22.

comps.label: Special elections
comps.note: Democrats have beaten the 2024 presidential margin by 12.5 points in this cycle's special elections. In 2006, 2018 and 2022 specials overstated the eventual swing by 3.9 points on average, so that much is taken off.

comps.label: 2025 Virginia and New Jersey governors
comps.note: Both states moved 9.0 points toward Democrats from 2024. The off-year governor races have pointed the right way before every midterm since 2006, with large misses in size.
